beats.intro: Chapter six, lesson eight. Cell walls, the extracellular matrix, and cell junctions. [[map]]Here is our tour map of the cell, and this is the last stop. So far we have stayed inside. [[out]]Now the camera pulls out, to the cell's outside, and to its {{neighbors|neighbours}}. [[celery]]Snap a stalk of celery, and it is crisp, because its cells are boxed in by walls. [[skin]]Skin and the lining of your gut hold together for a different reason. They are cells fastened to each other, and to a matrix. [[three]]So there are three things to meet. Plant cell walls, the animal extracellular matrix, and junctions between cells.
beats.walls: Start with the wall. [[who]]Plants have cell walls. So do prokaryotes, fungi, and some protists. Animal cells do not. [[jobs]]A wall protects the cell, and maintains its shape. It also helps prevent excessive water uptake. [[swell]]A plant cell soaks up water and swells, until the wall pushes back. The wall does not keep water out. It stops the cell from bursting. [[made]]What is it made of? Cellulose fibers, embedded in other polysaccharides and protein. [[rebar]]Think of steel rods set in concrete. The fibers give strength, and the surrounding material fills the gaps.
beats.layers: Now look closely at a wall between two plant cells. [[mid]]Between the cells lies a thin layer called the middle lamella. It is the glue that holds {{neighbors|neighbours}} together. [[prim]]Next to the middle lamella, each cell has its primary cell wall. It is relatively thin and flexible, so a growing cell can still stretch. [[sec]]Some cells also add a secondary cell wall. It goes between the plasma membrane and the primary wall, and it is thick and strong. [[trunk]]That is why wood is hard. A tree trunk is mostly secondary walls. [[order]]So from the middle outward, it goes middle lamella, primary wall, secondary wall, and then the plasma membrane.
beats.plasmo: A wall is a barrier. So how do plant cells talk to each other? [[pore]]Through channels called plasmodesmata. [[line]]Each plasmodesma is a pore through the walls, lined by the plasma membrane, so the cytoplasm of one cell runs into its {{neighbor|neighbour}}'s. [[pass]]Water, small solutes, and even proteins and RNA can pass from one plant cell to the next. [[only]]Plasmodesmata belong to plants. Animal cells have other kinds of connections, and we meet them soon.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which layer lies between two adjacent plant cells?
beats.ecm: Animal cells have no wall, but they are not bare. [[matrix]]They are covered by an extracellular matrix, the E C M. [[coll]]Its main fiber is collagen, a strong, ropelike glycoprotein. [[fibro]]Fibronectin is another glycoprotein. It connects the matrix to the cell. [[proteo]]And proteoglycans are a core protein with many sugar chains attached, like a bottle brush. [[web]]Together they weave a web around the cell, a little like the filling in a mattress.
beats.integrin: How does the cell hold on to that web? [[integ]]With integrins. They are receptor proteins that span the plasma membrane. [[out]]On the outside, an integrin binds the matrix. [[in]]On the inside, it links to the microfilaments of the cytoskeleton. [[bridge]]So the matrix is tied to the cell's own scaffolding. A pull on the matrix can be felt inside the cell. [[four]]The matrix does four jobs. It gives support, and it helps cells adhere. It takes part in movement, and in regulation of what the cell does.
beats.junc: Cells in a tissue also touch each other directly. [[gut]]Take the lining of your gut. It is a sheet of cells, and the sheet must hold together, and keep the gut contents out. [[kinds]]{{Neighboring|Neighbouring}} cells adhere, interact, and communicate through intercellular junctions. [[plant]]Plants use plasmodesmata. Animals use three more. Tight junctions, desmosomes, and gap junctions.
beats.tight: First, the tight junction. [[press]]The membranes of two {{neighbors|neighbours}} are pressed together. [[leak]]Fluid trying to leak between the cells is stopped. [[seal]]So a tight junction seals the sheet, like the zipper on a sandwich bag. [[use]]That is how the gut lining keeps its contents from slipping through the gaps.
beats.desmo: Second, the desmosome. [[plaque]]It is a button-like plaque on each of two {{neighboring|neighbouring}} cells. [[if]]Intermediate filaments run into the plaques, like cables. [[rivet]]A desmosome is an anchoring junction. It rivets cells into strong sheets, so skin can be stretched without tearing apart.
beats.gap: Third, the gap junction. [[chan]]It is a channel that runs between the cytoplasm of two cells. [[small]]Small molecules and ions can pass through. [[heart]]In heart muscle, signals flow through gap junctions from cell to cell, so the cells beat together. [[name]]This is a communicating junction. It is the animal counterpart of plasmodesmata.
beats.q2: Quick check. Match each junction to its job.
beats.recap: That completes the tour. Let's walk the whole cell once more. [[nuc]]The nucleus is head office. It holds the DNA. [[ribo]]Ribosomes are the workbenches that build proteins. [[er]]The endoplasmic reticulum is the production line. [[golgi]]The Golgi apparatus sorts and ships. [[lyso]]Lysosomes and vacuoles recycle and store. [[mito]]Mitochondria and chloroplasts supply the energy. [[perox]]Peroxisomes handle the harmful peroxide. [[cyto]]The cytoskeleton is the scaffolding and the rails. [[outside]]And outside, the wall, the matrix, and the junctions tie it all into a tissue. [[end]]Now try the practice.

beats.finish: Well done. That's the end of chapter six, and of our tour of the cell.
